title: Federal Plan Mandates Steep Colorado River Water Cuts for California, Arizona and Nevada
excerpt: The Bureau of Reclamation's 10-year framework requires lower basin states to slash water use by up to 20% as reservoirs hit record lows, with deeper cuts possible through 2036.
body:
• The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation released a 10-year framework on Friday requiring California, Arizona and Nevada to cut Colorado River water use by 16 to 20% through 2028, with potential cuts of up to 3 million acre-feet per year through 2036.
  • The combined water stored in Lake Powell and Lake Mead hit a historic low on July 12, falling below levels not seen since the early 1960s, after the driest winter on record.
  • Arizona faces the steepest reductions — 760,000 acre-feet from its 2.8 million acre-foot share — and has warned the cuts could "devastate" its water users and economy.
  • Upper basin states (Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming) face no mandatory cuts under the plan, deepening a rift with lower basin states that may end up in court.

The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation on Friday published its final environmental impact statement for the Colorado River, a 10-year operating framework that will require California, Arizona and Nevada to slash their water use by 16 to 20% through 2028 — with far deeper cuts possible in later years as the Southwest's most critical water source spirals into crisis.

Under the plan, the three lower basin states could face collective reductions of up to 3 million acre-feet per year from 2029 through 2036, enough water to supply roughly 9 million American households. The framework replaces a 20-year agreement that expires at the end of 2026, after three years of deadlocked negotiations among the seven states that share the river failed to produce a consensus deal.

"This framework provides the flexibility to respond to changing hydrologic conditions while preserving the opportunity for the Basin States to continue working toward durable, consensus-based solutions."

— Doug Burgum, Secretary of the Interior

Record-Low Reservoirs Drive Federal Action

The Colorado River is the lifeblood of the American Southwest. It irrigates more than 5 million acres of farmland, generates hydropower for some 700,000 homes and provides drinking water to 40 million people across seven U.S. states, two Mexican states and Native American tribes. Today, 95% of the basin is in drought.

The combined water level in Lake Powell and Lake Mead — the river's two largest reservoirs and two of the biggest in the country — broke a historic low on July 12, falling below levels not seen since several years before Glen Canyon Dam began collecting water in the early 1960s. Lake Mead is on track to tumble to its lowest level on record as early as next week, and Lake Powell could reach "minimum power pool" — the threshold below which Glen Canyon Dam can no longer generate hydropower — by spring 2027.

The crisis was compounded by the driest winter on record across the western United States, which left the region in a severe snow drought and forced the Bureau of Reclamation to release water early from an upstream reservoir, Flaming Gorge in Wyoming, to keep Lake Powell's turbines turning.

Who Bears the Pain

The 1922 Colorado River Compact divides the river's water equally between upper and lower basins, allotting 7.5 million acre-feet per year to each. But as flows have dwindled, the lower basin states — which consume the bulk of the water, primarily for sprawling farms and booming cities — have been forced to shoulder nearly all the reductions.

Arizona faces the steepest cuts: 760,000 acre-feet from its 2.8 million acre-foot annual share, a consequence of a 1960s-era deal that placed its Central Arizona Project canal at a lower priority than California's supply. California would surrender 444,000 acre-feet from its 4.4 million share, while Nevada, with a comparatively small 300,000 acre-foot share, would give up 50,000.

The Arizona Department of Water Resources pushed back sharply, saying the framework "does nothing to elevate expectations around a coherent seven-state plan for shared sacrifice" and warning that the proposed reductions "would devastate Arizona's water users and its economy."

The upper basin states of Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming face no mandatory cuts under the plan, a disparity that has deepened the interstate rift. Upper basin officials argue they already endure reduced supplies from decades of drought and lack the large reservoirs that buffer lower basin states.

"If you don't rebuild storage and we keep living on the edge of disaster, one of these days we're going to have such a dry year that it all goes to hell — and that's exactly what happened."

— Jack Schmidt, Utah State University researcher

A Two-Year Planning Cycle

Rather than locking in rules for a decade or more, the Trump administration opted for a framework reviewed every two years, giving the government flexibility to adapt to changing conditions. Federal officials are expected to publish the first specific operating plan in the coming days, covering 2027 and 2028. New rules must be in place by October 1, the start of the 2027 water year.

But the approach has drawn criticism for leaving water users and cities without long-term certainty. Sarah Porter, director of Arizona State University's Kyl Center for Water Policy, noted the tension: "The Bureau's desire for maximum flexibility is in tension with the Lower Basin states' need for certainty."

What Comes Next

States can continue negotiating, and any consensus deal could supplant the federal plan. But few observers are optimistic. The states have been unable to agree after three years of talks, and the prospect of litigation looms. Arizona has warned that a legal challenge could follow if 10-year average flows into the lower basin fall below what the compact mandates — a threshold expected to be crossed for the first time this year.

For the roughly 4 million Indian Americans living in the affected Southwest metros of Phoenix, Las Vegas, and the Los Angeles basin, the cuts will translate into stricter water use rules and potentially higher utility bills. Agriculture-dependent communities across the region — and the food supply chains they feed — face an even more uncertain future.
nri_angle: Indian Americans concentrated in Phoenix, Las Vegas and Southern California metro areas face water use restrictions and likely rate hikes as the federal government mandates steep cuts to Colorado River allocations.
